cases.label: two_sum_hashmap
cases.stem: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Talk me through your approach.
cases.reference_answer: Walk the array once, keeping a hash map from value to index. For each element x at index i, look up target - x in the map; if it is there, return that index and i. Otherwise store x -> i and continue. One pass, O(n) time and O(n) space. The map lookup is average O(1) because the key is hashed to a bucket; worst case is O(n) per lookup if every key collides, which is why the average-case claim needs the hash function to distribute well.

key_points.statement: Solves it in a single pass over the array
Uses a hash map from value to index
Looks up the complement, target minus the current value
States the time complexity as O(n)
Acknowledges hash map lookup is O(1) on average, not worst case

cases.label: hashmap_lookup_why
cases.stem: Why is hash map lookup O(1)?
cases.reference_answer: The key is passed through a hash function that maps it to a bucket index, so finding the bucket is a constant-time computation rather than a search. Within a bucket you still compare keys, so the constant-time claim holds only while buckets stay short — which requires a good hash function and a bounded load factor, with resizing when it is exceeded. If every key collides into one bucket the lookup degrades to O(n), so O(1) is the average case, not a guarantee.

key_points.statement: A hash function maps the key to a bucket index
Collisions are handled by chaining or probing
Worst case is O(n); O(1) is the average case
The average case depends on load factor and a good hash function

answers.label: hashmap_full_credit
answers.question: hashmap_lookup_why
answers.note: Mechanism, limits, and when it is wrong — a 4 on depth.
answers.text: Because the key gets run through a hash function that turns it into a bucket index, so you jump straight to the bucket instead of scanning. Inside the bucket you still compare keys, so it stays constant only while buckets are short, which is why implementations resize once the load factor goes past a threshold. If the hash function is bad and everything lands in one bucket you are back to O(n) — so O(1) is average case, not a guarantee.

answers.label: verbose_but_empty
answers.question: hashmap_lookup_why
answers.note: §12 adversarial — long, fluent, covers no key point. Length must not buy a score.
answers.text: That is a really good question and honestly it is one of those things that comes up all the time in interviews, so I have thought about it quite a lot. Hash maps are one of the most important data structures you can learn, and I would say that understanding them properly is genuinely one of the highest leverage things a student can do. They are used absolutely everywhere in real systems, in databases, in caches, in compilers, in basically every standard library you can name. The reason people like them so much is that they are just very fast compared to the alternatives, and speed is what matters when you are working at scale. So when someone asks why lookup is fast, I think the honest answer is that it is because hash maps are designed to be fast, and that design is what makes them so widely used in practice.

answers.label: confidently_wrong
answers.question: hashmap_lookup_why
answers.note: §12 adversarial — fluent and false. Evidence must cite the false claim.
answers.text: Hash map lookup is O(1) guaranteed in every case, that is the whole point of the structure — unlike a tree it never degrades. The hash function is a perfect one-to-one mapping so two different keys can never land in the same bucket, which is why collisions are not something you have to handle.

answers.text: So the amortised constant time comes from the load factor and the bucket array and the collision resolution strategy, and open addressing with linear probing gives you cache locality, and then the hash function distributes uniformly across the keyspace which is the invariant, so the complexity is O(1) amortised over the resize.

answers.label: two_sum_full_credit
answers.question: two_sum_hashmap
answers.note: Correct approach, stated complexity, handles the constraint.
answers.text: One pass with a hash map from value to index. For each element I compute target minus that element and check whether it is already in the map; if it is, I have my pair and I return the stored index and the current one. If not I put the current value and index in and move on. That is O(n) time and O(n) space, and it handles duplicates correctly because I check before inserting.
